newsitem.title: UK: ENEL fuel oil price squeeze to worsen.
newsitem.headline: ENEL fuel oil price squeeze to worsen.

text.p: Italy's state power utility ENEL, the world's biggest buyer of fuel oil, will spend 1997 honing the secretive buying tactics that have given it a stranglehold on the European fuel oil market, traders say.

Buyers at the Italian power generator will use their continually falling demand for fuel, as alternative energy sources come on stream, to squeeze better bargains from suppliers, Italian oil industry and market sources say.
"They (Enel) have run the fuel oil market for the past three to four months," said a trader with a British oil major.
"They have a much more successful strategy than before."

Italian oil industry newsletter Staffetta Quotidiana said last month Enel's overall fuel oil purchases would fall by 13.7 percent this year, from 22.6 to 19.5 million tonnes, as emission laws and costs force it to burn more gas.
Enel will import some 3.4 million tonnes less fuel oil in 1997 than in 1996, the journal said, with the majority of that cutback coming in the one percent grade largely supplied from northern Europe.

Having long been a by-word for over-paying, ENEL now exercises such tight price control it has effectively killed the market in European low sulphur fuel, traders say, since very few alternative buyers exist.

"They're doing a very good job by getting traders out of the market and establishing long-term contracts directly with refiners," said one supplier. "The low sulphur market is almost completely illiquid."

By insisting on keeping deals confidential Enel ensures sellers are largely unaware of demand, often allowing the company to dictate prices for the prompt cargoes which it picks off the bottom of the market.
By actively talking prices down Enel at least counters, if not prevents, bullish market comment from buoying the reference quotes used for pricing term deals.
"Refiners are just dumping their low sulphur and getting on with making profits from other products," said one producer. "We're going to have problems with low sulphur all this year."
Enel now more frequently reviews the terms of its longer contracts with major suppliers.
"They (Enel) are periodically walking away from arrangements, which spooks the market," said one broker.

Enel's drastic cutbacks and its ability to stagger its purchasing until it sees prices fall were partly to blame for the sharp drop in fuel oil values earlier this year, at a time when winter demand should have lent support.
"Fuel oil held its normal seasonal pattern until December and then it flipped to weaken when you'd expect its strength to persist," said energy analyst Colin Birch of Purvin and Gertz in London.
Low sulphur has lost $40 a tonne in value since December and now trades at levels not seen since July 1995.
Its sharp fall came four months earlier than in past years, although much of that can be attributed to crude's 30 percent slide this year.

However low sulphur has continued falling in price while high sulphur cracked cargoes, which have a more diverse customer base, bottomed out in March. Low sulphur may still have further to go, some traders say.
With Italian power demand falling as summer approaches and industrial production declines in a near-recession environment there is no suggestion ENEL will buy more fuel.

"They buy one or two cargoes a week, they are never out of the market," said an Italian oil industry analyst who follows Enel. "But there is absolutely no need to buy more fuel oil because of weak electricity demand."

While in the long term anti-pollution legislation may force high sulphur users to switch to low sulphur fuel, for now low sulphur sellers must deal with Enel or try to market the fuel out of the region, traders say. - Sean Maguire, London newsroom +44 171 542 8060
